title: Reusable building blocks
scopeHtml: Scope: fan-out on write/read, sharded counters, bloom filter, HyperLogLog, count-min sketch, geohash and quadtree.

notes.title: Why reusable building blocks
notes.html:
Most system design problems are the same few patterns in different clothes: spread work, count things, test membership, find nearby things. Knowing the blocks lets you assemble answers quickly and justify each choice with numbers.

This chapter: fan-out on write vs read (feeds), sharded counters (hot counts), Bloom filter (cheap "have I seen this?"), HyperLogLog (count unique), Count-Min Sketch (frequency, top-K), geohash and quadtree (nearby search). The last four are probabilistic data structures: they trade a small, bounded error for huge memory savings.

Worked example. Counting unique visitors per page across 1B pageviews/day: an exact set of user ids is 1B x 8 B = 8 GB per day per page group. HyperLogLog does it in 12 KB per counter with about 0.8% error. That 6-orders-of-magnitude saving is the whole point.

Industry examples. Redis ships HyperLogLog, Bloom (module), geo commands; Cassandra and HBase use Bloom filters per SSTable/HFile; Twitter and Instagram built feed fan-out; Uber uses H3 (hex grid) for geo.

Decision gravity. These are usually implementation details and reversible, but the choice of fan-out strategy shapes storage, write cost and latency and is hard to change after launch.

Everyday analogy. A toolbox: you do not forge a new hammer for each nail.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an exact structure when an approximate one is fine (and vice versa for money or legal counts).
  • Not stating the error rate and the memory used.

notes.title: Fan-out on write (push)
notes.html:
On a new post, immediately copy a reference to it into every follower's precomputed feed. Reads become a single cheap lookup.

Mechanism: user A posts; a worker looks up A's followers and, for each, does LPUSH feed:{follower} post_id (Redis list/sorted set, capped at 800 to 1,000 entries). Reading a feed = LRANGE feed:{me} 0 49 then hydrate post bodies in one batch (multi-get). Writes are asynchronous via a queue (Kafka), so posting stays fast.

# per follower
ZADD feed:1002 1731146400 post:9981
ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:1002 0 -801     # keep latest 800
# read
ZREVRANGE feed:1002 0 49

Worked example. Average user has 200 followers, 5M posts/day: 5M x 200 = 1B feed insertions/day, about 11.6k/s average, 35k/s peak. Each entry ~16 B + Redis overhead ~ 50 B: 1B x 50 B = 50 GB of daily churn into a bounded set (800 per user x 100M active users x 50 B = 4 TB of feed cache, sharded across the cluster). Read: 1 Redis call plus 1 batch hydrate, under 20 ms.

Industry examples. Twitter's timeline (Redis-backed home timeline per user), Instagram's early feed, Facebook's news feed for ordinary users, WhatsApp-style delivery to inboxes.

Decision gravity. Great when reads greatly outnumber writes and follower counts are modest. Breaks for celebrities (see below) and wastes work for inactive followers. Reversible with effort, but data layout (precomputed lists) must be rebuilt.

Everyday analogy. A newsletter: the publisher prints and drops a copy in every subscriber's mailbox the moment it is written; reading is instant.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring celebrities (a 100M-follower post means 100M writes).
  • Fanning out to inactive users; skip users not active in 30 days and build their feed on login.
  • Storing full post bodies in feeds instead of ids.

notes.title: Fan-out on read (pull) and the hybrid
notes.html:
On read, fetch recent posts from everyone the user follows and merge them. Writes are cheap (just store the post); reads do the work.

Mechanism: a read queries following list (say 300 accounts), fetches each account's latest N posts (from a per-author timeline), and merge-sorts by time (priority queue). Cache the result for a few seconds. Cost scales with number of followees, not followers.

Hybrid (what Twitter did): push for normal users, pull for celebrities. At read time, take the precomputed feed (pushed items) and merge in recent posts from the few celebrities the user follows. The cutoff is e.g. followers above 100k to 1M.

fun homeFeed(me: Long): List<Post> {
    val pushed = redis.zrevrange("feed:$me", 0, 99)                 // ids
    val celebs = following(me).filter { isCelebrity(it) }
        .flatMap { redis.zrevrange("timeline:$it", 0, 19) }          // pull side
    return hydrate((pushed + celebs).sortedByDescending(::ts).take(50))
}

Worked example. Celebrity with 50M followers posts. Push would cost 50M writes (at 100k writes/s, that is 500 s, and a spike). Pull: the post is stored once; each of 50M followers' next read adds one small merge (about 2 extra Redis calls). Reads happen over hours, spreading the load.

Industry examples. Twitter (hybrid after celebrity hot spots), Instagram and Facebook (ranking with ML on top of candidate sets), Pinterest (smart feed), LinkedIn feed.

Decision gravity. The cutoff threshold is tunable and reversible; moving between pure push and pure pull is not (different storage). Hybrid is the safe interview answer if you explain both costs.

Everyday analogy. A library vs a newsletter: with pull you walk the shelves of every author you follow when you visit.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring one strategy "the answer" without discussing follower distribution.
  • Forgetting ranking: chronological merge is rarely the final product.
  • Unfollow/delete handling: lazy filtering at read time is easier than deleting from millions of feeds.

notes.title: Sharded counters
notes.html:
When many writers increment the same counter, one row or key becomes a hot spot; split it into N shards, increment a random one, and sum on read.

Mechanism: key likes:post9 becomes likes:post9:0..N-1. A write picks shard = random(N) (or hash of the user id) and does INCR. Read = sum of N shards (MGET), optionally cached for seconds, or maintained as a periodically rolled-up total. Also use write batching: buffer increments in memory/Redis and flush aggregates to the database every second.

INCR likes:post9:3                # write
MGET likes:post9:0 likes:post9:1 likes:post9:2 likes:post9:3   # read, then sum
-- relational version
UPDATE counter_shards SET n = n + 1 WHERE counter_id = 9 AND shard = floor(random()*10)::int;
SELECT sum(n) FROM counter_shards WHERE counter_id = 9;

Worked example. A single row in Postgres tolerates about 1k to 2k updates/s (row lock serialises writes). A viral post gets 50k likes/s. With 50 shards, each takes 1k/s, safe. Read cost: sum of 50 values, ~1 ms, cached. Accuracy: briefly stale but eventually exact.

Industry examples. Google Cloud Datastore/Firestore document the sharded counter pattern (1 write/s per document limit); Instagram/Twitter like and view counts; YouTube view counts are intentionally delayed and batched (they froze at 301 historically for verification); DynamoDB write sharding with a suffix.

Decision gravity. Shard count N is adjustable (more shards later) as long as readers sum all existing ones. It trades read cost and exactness for write throughput; the one-way part is giving up simple "read one value".

Everyday analogy. Ten tally clerks at a stadium gate each counting a part of the crowd; add their sheets at the end instead of everyone queuing at one clipboard.

Common interview traps.

  • Sharding counters that are not actually hot.
  • Needing exactness for money (use a ledger, not an approximate counter).
  • Fixing a hot key by only adding replicas (writes still hit the one primary).

notes.title: Bloom filter
notes.html:
A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this item?" using a tiny bit array: it can say "definitely not" or "probably yes". No false negatives, a tunable false-positive rate, no deletions (in the basic form).

Mechanism: a bit array of m bits, k hash functions. Add: set the k bits h1(x)..hk(x). Check: if any of the k bits is 0, the item is definitely absent; if all 1, it is probably present. Sizing for n items and false-positive rate p: m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 bits (about 9.6 bits per item at p = 1%), and k = (m/n) ln 2 (about 7). Variants: counting Bloom filters (support delete), cuckoo filters (delete, often smaller), scalable Bloom filters (grow).

p = 1%   -> 9.6 bits/item, k = 7
p = 0.1% -> 14.4 bits/item, k = 10
1 billion URLs at 1%: ~1.2 GB (vs ~64 GB storing 64-byte URLs)
import math
def size(n, p):
    m = math.ceil(-n * math.log(p) / (math.log(2) ** 2))
    return m, round(m / n * math.log(2))
print(size(1_000_000_000, 0.01))   # (9585058378, 7)  about 1.2 GB, 7 hashes

Worked example. Cassandra read: a key may live in any of 10 SSTables. Without Bloom filters it does up to 10 disk reads for a missing key (10 x 100 us = 1 ms+). With a 1% filter per SSTable, a missing key triggers about 0.1 false disk reads on average. Chrome's old Safe Browsing check and CDN "one-hit-wonder" cache admission use the same trick.

Industry examples. Cassandra, HBase, LevelDB/RocksDB per-SSTable filters; Medium's "don't recommend articles already read"; Google Bigtable; Akamai cache admission; web crawler "visited URLs" sets; Bitcoin SPV clients; Redis Stack BF.ADD / BF.EXISTS; username availability pre-checks.

Decision gravity. Easy, reversible optimisation in front of an expensive lookup. Size it for the future (a filter over capacity sees false positives rise sharply) and plan to rebuild periodically.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer with a rough guest list sketch: if your name's marks are not on it, you are definitely not invited; if they are, he checks the real list.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a "yes" is certain.
  • Deleting from a plain Bloom filter (corrupts it; use counting or cuckoo).
  • Forgetting that the filter is only a gate; the authoritative check must follow for "probably yes".

notes.title: HyperLogLog
notes.html:
HyperLogLog (HLL) estimates the number of distinct items (cardinality) using a few KB regardless of how many items you see. Standard error is about 1.04 / sqrt(m).

Mechanism: hash every item to 64 bits. Use the first p bits to choose one of m = 2^p registers; in the rest, count leading zeros plus one and keep the maximum per register. Intuition: seeing a hash with many leading zeros is rare (like flipping 20 heads in a row), so the longest streak suggests how many distinct items were hashed. The estimate is a harmonic mean across registers with bias corrections. HLLs are mergeable (take the max per register), so you can count uniques per hour and union them for the day without double counting.

PFADD uv:2026-11-09:page1 user1 user2 user3
PFCOUNT uv:2026-11-09:page1
PFMERGE uv:2026-11-week uv:2026-11-09:page1 uv:2026-11-10:page1

Worked example. Redis HLL uses 16,384 registers (p = 14) of 6 bits = 12 KB per counter, standard error 0.81%. Counting 1B unique users: exact set at 8 B each = 8 GB; HLL = 12 KB, error ~ +/-8M. 100,000 pages x 12 KB = 1.2 GB for per-page unique visitors, easily held in memory.

Industry examples. Redis (PFADD), Google BigQuery APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT (HLL++), Presto/Trino, Druid, Snowflake HLL, Facebook and Twitter analytics, Reddit view counts (as "unique viewers").

Decision gravity. Reversible and cheap; use whenever "about" is acceptable (analytics, dashboards, capacity). Use exact counting for billing or legal obligations. You cannot list members or remove items from an HLL.

Everyday analogy. Guessing the size of a crowd from the longest streak of coin heads anyone achieved; with many tries, longer streaks appear.

Common interview traps.

  • Using HLL when you need membership ("was user X counted?"): that is Bloom's job.
  • Summing HLL counts from different sets instead of merging registers (double counts overlaps).
  • Using it for small sets where exact counting is cheap.

notes.title: Count-Min Sketch and top-K
notes.html:
A Count-Min Sketch (CMS) estimates how many times each item appeared, in fixed memory. It never undercounts; it may overcount slightly because of hash collisions.

Mechanism: a 2D array of counters, d rows by w columns, with d independent hash functions. Update(x): for each row i, increment table[i][h_i(x)]. Estimate(x): take the minimum of the d counters (collisions only add, so the minimum is the least inflated). Error bound: estimate <= true + epsilon * N with probability 1 - delta, where w = ceil(e / epsilon) and d = ceil(ln(1/delta)). For top-K (heavy hitters) combine a CMS with a small min-heap: on each event update the sketch, estimate the count, and keep the K largest in the heap.

import heapq, mmh3
class CMS:
    def __init__(s, w=2000, d=5): s.w, s.d, s.t = w, d, [[0]*w for _ in range(d)]
    def add(s, x):  [s.t[i].__setitem__(mmh3.hash(x, i) % s.w, s.t[i][mmh3.hash(x, i) % s.w] + 1) for i in range(s.d)]
    def est(s, x):  return min(s.t[i][mmh3.hash(x, i) % s.w] for i in range(s.d))

Worked example. Trending hashtags over 1B events/hour. Choose epsilon = 0.0001 (error up to 100k on 1B events for rare items; heavy hitters are far larger), delta = 0.01: w = 27,183, d = 5, so 5 x 27k x 4 B = 540 KB total. An exact map of 100M distinct tags at about 50 B each = 5 GB. Merge sketches from many servers by adding the arrays cell-wise.

Industry examples. Twitter trending topics and heavy hitters, Redis Stack CMS.INCRBY/TOPK, network traffic monitors (heavy flows), Apache DataSketches, rate limiting for huge key sets, Facebook's frequency estimation for ads. Related alternatives: Space-Saving / Misra-Gries algorithms for exact-ish top-K with counters.

Decision gravity. Fine and reversible when approximate popularity is enough; wrong for per-user billing. Always report that counts may be inflated for low-frequency items.

Everyday analogy. Several noisy tally boards where different words sometimes share a box; to guess a word's count you trust the board that is least crowded for it (the minimum).

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting underestimates (it only overestimates).
  • Using CMS for rare items (collision noise swamps small counts); it shines on heavy hitters.
  • Confusing it with Bloom (membership) and HLL (distinct count).

notes.title: Geohash and quadtree
notes.html:
To find "places near me" fast, convert 2D locations into something an index can search: a geohash string or a quadtree cell.

Geohash: interleave the bits of latitude and longitude ranges (repeatedly halving) and encode in base32. Nearby points share a prefix; longer prefix = smaller cell. Precision: 4 chars about 39 km x 20 km, 5 chars about 4.9 km x 4.9 km, 6 chars about 1.2 km x 0.6 km, 7 chars about 153 m x 153 m, 8 chars about 38 m x 19 m. Store geohash in an indexed column, query LIKE 'u4pru%' (prefix range scan) plus the 8 neighbouring cells (to fix boundary issues), then filter by exact distance (Haversine). Redis geo uses a 52-bit geohash in a sorted set (GEOADD, GEOSEARCH).

Quadtree: recursively split a square into 4 quadrants until each leaf has at most K points (for example 100). Dense areas (city centres) get deep trees, empty areas stay shallow. Search: descend to the leaf containing the query point, then look at neighbouring leaves. In-memory (rebuild or incrementally update), good for heavy skew. Alternatives: S2 (Google, cells on a sphere, used by Foursquare/Uber earlier), H3 (Uber, hexagons with uniform neighbour distance), PostGIS with GiST/R-tree.

-- geohash prefix search plus exact filter
SELECT id FROM drivers
WHERE geohash LIKE ANY (ARRAY['u4pru%','u4prv%', /* + 7 neighbours */ 'u4prt%'])
  AND ST_DistanceSphere(loc, ST_MakePoint(:lng,:lat)) < 2000
ORDER BY ST_DistanceSphere(loc, ST_MakePoint(:lng,:lat)) LIMIT 10;
GEOADD drivers 77.5946 12.9716 d123
GEOSEARCH drivers FROMLONLAT 77.59 12.97 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 10

Worked example. 1M drivers, location updates every 4 s = 250k writes/s. Keep live positions in Redis/in-memory grid sharded by geohash prefix (one shard per city-ish prefix) so a query touches 1 to 9 cells. A 2 km search with 6-char cells (about 1.2 km) reads 9 cells, each holding tens of drivers, rather than scanning 1M. Quadtree leaf limit 100 points: Manhattan splits deeply, a desert stays one cell.

Industry examples. Uber (H3 hex grid, driver dispatch), Lyft, Yelp/Foursquare (S2/geohash for places), Google Maps (S2), Elasticsearch geo_point and geo_shape, MongoDB 2dsphere, DoorDash and Swiggy delivery-partner matching, Tinder.

Decision gravity. Cell size and index choice are reversible but require reindexing; shard by geohash prefix creates hot shards in dense cities, so split by load not area (adaptive quadtree/S2 level choice). Edge cases: boundary crossing, the poles, and the antimeridian.

Everyday analogy. Postal codes: letters whose codes begin the same are in the same area, so you only check neighbouring districts instead of every house.

Common interview traps.

  • Searching a single geohash cell and missing close points just across the border (query neighbours too).
  • Assuming geohash cells are square and equal size (they stretch toward the poles).
  • Using plain lat/lng B-tree range queries on two columns (inefficient; use a spatial index).
  • Uniform grids for skewed density (use quadtree or adaptive levels).

notes.title: Choosing a block quickly
notes.html:
Match the question in the prompt to the structure.

Interview signal Block Memory / cost sense
"News feed / timeline" Fan-out (hybrid) 1B feed writes/day for 5M posts x 200 followers
"Like counts, view counts, hot key" Sharded counter N shards, sum on read
"Have we seen this URL / username / event?" Bloom filter about 10 bits per item at 1%
"Unique visitors / distinct users" HyperLogLog 12 KB per counter, 0.81%
"Trending / most frequent / heavy hitters" Count-Min Sketch + heap hundreds of KB
"Nearby drivers / restaurants" Geohash / quadtree / S2 / H3 prefix scan on neighbouring cells

Worked example. Design "post analytics": views (sharded counter, exact-ish), uniques (HLL per post per day), top referrers (CMS + heap), "already viewed by me?" (Bloom filter per user in Redis), nearby events (geohash). Memory per post-day: counters 1 KB + HLL 12 KB + sketch 100 KB, so 1M posts = about 113 GB, shardable across a small Redis cluster.

Decision gravity. Prefer exact structures until the numbers say otherwise (memory, hot keys, latency); introduce approximations where the business tolerates a stated error.

Everyday analogy. Knowing which kitchen gadget to grab: peeler, grater, or blender, instead of using a knife for everything.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming the structure without saying its error, memory and failure modes.
  • Applying probabilistic structures to correctness-critical data (payments, inventory).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Fan-out on write precomputes feeds (fast reads, huge writes for celebrities); fan-out on read merges at query time; hybrid pushes for normal users and pulls for celebrities.
  • Sharded counters split a hot key into N parts, random increment, sum on read; batch writes to the database.
  • Bloom filter: bit array + k hashes, no false negatives, about 9.6 bits per item at 1% false positives, no deletes (use counting or cuckoo variants).
  • HyperLogLog: distinct counts in about 12 KB with ~0.8% error, mergeable by register max; cannot test membership.
  • Count-Min Sketch: frequency estimates that only overcount, take the min across rows; pair with a heap for top-K.
  • Geohash (prefix = proximity, query neighbour cells) and quadtree/S2/H3 (adaptive cells) turn nearby search into index lookups; shard by cell with attention to dense-city hot spots.
  • Always state the error rate, memory use and what the structure cannot do.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Bloom filter, what guarantees does it give, and where is it used?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic building block; the key signal is knowing the one-sided error.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions that answers "is this key in the set?" with either "definitely not" or "probably yes". It has no false negatives, only false positives, and uses a few bits per element. You can add but not remove (a counting variant allows removal). It sits in front of an expensive lookup: Cassandra and LSM stores use one per SSTable to skip disk reads for missing keys.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Add: set k bits at positions h1(x)..hk(x). Query: all k bits set means "maybe", any zero means "no".

bits: 0 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 ...   add("a") sets positions 1,4,7
query("b") -> position 2 is 0 -> definitely not present

Sizing rule of thumb: about 9.6 bits per element for 1% false positive rate with k about 7, so 100M keys is about 120 MB. Example: a Cassandra read may touch 10 SSTables; without filters a missing key costs up to 10 disk reads, with a 1% filter about 0.1 false reads on average. Over capacity, false positives rise sharply, so size for growth and rebuild periodically.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it where false positives are unacceptable without a confirm step.
  • Under-sizing, so the false positive rate drifts up.
  • Expecting deletes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you delete? -> Counting Bloom filter or a cuckoo filter, or rebuild.
  2. Where else? -> Safe-browsing prechecks, "already seen" crawler URLs, cache admission to skip one-hit wonders.
  3. How do you choose k and m? -> Derive from n and target p; more bits lowers p.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "probabilistic set". Senior: one-sided error, sizing math, rebuild policy and what happens after a false positive.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An undersized filter in front of a cache doubled DB load after traffic growth.

questions.promptHtml: What does HyperLogLog do, and what do you give up when using it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the approximation trade-off and knowing what cannot be done.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements using tiny, fixed memory. Redis HLL uses 12 KB per counter with about 0.81% standard error, regardless of whether you count a thousand or a billion items. The idea: hash each item, track the longest run of leading zeros per register; rare long runs imply many distinct items. You give up exactness, membership listing and removal. Counters merge by taking register-wise maximum, which makes it great for unions across servers or days.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Exact unique visitors: 1B users x 8 B = 8 GB. HLL: 12 KB with error about plus or minus 8M at 1B. 100,000 pages x 12 KB = 1.2 GB for per-page unique visitors, held in memory.

PFADD page:42:2024-06-01 user123 user456
PFCOUNT page:42:2024-06-01
PFMERGE week:42 page:42:2024-06-01 page:42:2024-06-02   # union of days

Not suitable for billing or legal counts. Intersections need inclusion-exclusion and are inaccurate.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it for billing.
  • Expecting to list members.
  • Computing intersections of small overlaps.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you do weekly uniques? -> Merge daily HLLs.
  2. Why not a set? -> Memory grows linearly with cardinality.
  3. Error at small cardinalities? -> Implementations use exact or sparse modes for small counts (verify per implementation).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "approximate unique count". Senior: error bounds, merge, where exact counts are required.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard moved from COUNT(DISTINCT) over billions of rows to per-day HLL and went from minutes to milliseconds.

questions.contextHtml: A social feed app: 100M active users, average 200 followers, 5M posts/day, peak 3x average. Feed shows the latest 800 post ids per user kept in Redis. Read SLO: p99 under 50 ms. Entry cost is about 50 B in Redis including overhead. The architect asks whether push is feasible and what it costs.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is fast, so yes" without numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Distribution of followers (celebrities)? Inactive users? Freshness requirement? Ranking?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); start with push for normal users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: push is feasible for average users; the tail breaks it.
  4. How I'd verify: follower-count histogram, load test.
  5. Root cause of design choice: reads outnumber writes, so precompute.
  6. Fix: writes: 5M x 200 = 1B feed insertions/day, about 11.6k/s average, about 35k/s peak. Storage: 800 x 100M x 50 B = 4 TB of feed cache, sharded (for example 40 nodes of 100 GB, verify node sizing). Daily churn 1B x 50 B = 50 GB into a bounded list. Read: 1 Redis call plus 1 batch hydrate, under 20 ms. Skip inactive users (do not push to users inactive for 30 days; build on login).
  7. Prevention: monitor queue lag of the fan-out workers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: pure push for everyone, because a 50M follower account breaks it (see hybrid).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Follow a new account? -> Backfill recent posts.
  • Delete a post? -> Remove from lists lazily, filter at hydrate time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team skipped inactive users and cut feed storage by 40%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers.
  • Hire: correct QPS and storage math.
  • Strong hire: inactive skip, backfill, delete handling, mentions celebrity problem.

questions.promptHtml: How do sharded counters work and what do you trade for the write throughput?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Hot-key handling is a staple of scale questions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One counter row serialises writes on a row lock, so a single row tolerates roughly 1k to 2k updates per second. I split the counter into N shards, write to a random shard, and read by summing all N. With 50 shards, 50k likes/s means about 1k/s per shard. I trade simple reads and instant exactness for write throughput: reads sum N values, usually cached, and may be briefly stale but eventually exact.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
-- write: pick shard = random(0..49)
UPDATE like_counts SET n = n + 1 WHERE post_id = 7 AND shard = 13;
-- read:
SELECT sum(n) FROM like_counts WHERE post_id = 7;

Alternatives: batch increments in memory and flush every second, or Redis INCR. N can grow later as long as readers sum all existing shards. Only apply shards to hot keys; most posts need one.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sharding every counter (read cost for no benefit).
  • Using it where exact-at-every-moment values are required.
  • Forgetting idempotency for retried likes (need a unique (user, post) set).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to prevent double likes? -> A (user_id, post_id) unique record; the counter is derived.
  2. Read cost? -> Sum of N, cache for 1 s.
  3. Can you reduce N? -> Merge shards into one during a quiet period.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "split the row". Senior: hot-key detection, caching sums, idempotency and eventual exactness.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A viral post's single counter row became a lock queue until sharded.

questions.contextHtml:
A viral video receives 50k likes/s. Postgres UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = $1 shows:

lock wait: 12.4s on relation posts, tuple (4411,7)
pg_stat_activity: 1,800 sessions waiting, app connection pool exhausted
db cpu 22%, iops normal

All API endpoints now time out; the team suspects a DB upgrade from last week and wants to roll it back.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Roll back the upgrade or add DB CPU.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which row do waiters target? Is likes stored on the post row (also read-heavy)? Is the video a single hot key?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Buffer likes in Redis (INCR) and flush to the DB in batches; shed duplicate likes; raise pool or kill waiting sessions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: row-lock contention on one row (low CPU and IOPS point to it); the upgrade (red herring); pool exhaustion as a symptom.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_locks blocking chain, group waiters by key.
  5. Root cause: 50k updates/s on one row, which tolerates about 1-2k/s.
  6. Fix: short term: Redis counter with periodic flush. Long term: sharded counter for hot posts (50 shards = about 1k/s each); the post row no longer takes the like writes; reads served from cache summing shards.
  7. Prevention: hot key detection and a load test with a skewed key.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not roll back; the upgrade did not cause it. Likes may lag by a second.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Redis down? -> Fallback shards in DB; accept loss of a few seconds of likes.
  • Unlike? -> Decrement with the same sharding and a unique (user, post) record.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rollback consumed 40 minutes and changed nothing, because the symptom was one row.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rollback or scale DB.
  • Hire: spots row contention and shards or buffers.
  • Strong hire: idempotency, hot-key detection, fallback behaviour.

questions.contextHtml:
A signup service uses a Bloom filter of taken usernames in front of the DB check. Sized for 10M names at 1% false positive. Two years on there are 38M names. Complaint volume: "username taken" shown for names that are free, up to 25% of attempts. DB load for existence checks also rose.

filter: m=96M bits, k=7, inserted=38M
estimated false positive rate ~ 90%+

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bloom filters are probabilistic, so that's expected."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What happens on "maybe"? Does the app trust the filter alone? Can the filter be rebuilt from the DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: On "maybe present" always confirm in the DB (never reject on the filter alone); this fixes correctness.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: over capacity: false positives rise sharply when n greatly exceeds the sizing; k mis-tuned for the new n.
  4. How I'd verify: measure fill ratio (set bits / total), sample queries for names known absent.
  5. Root cause: the filter was sized for 10M and holds 38M; nearly all bits are set.
  6. Fix: rebuild with m for 100M at 1%: about 9.6 bits x 100M = 960M bits = about 120 MB, k about 7; or a scalable Bloom filter with chained layers; rebuild on schedule when fill passes 50%.
  7. Prevention: alert on fill ratio and estimated false positive rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not use the filter as the source of truth; for "taken", the DB unique index decides.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Usernames released? -> Bloom cannot delete; periodic rebuild or a counting filter.
  • Memory tight? -> Use a cuckoo filter if deletes are needed (verify trade-offs).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "false positive" bug was nine months of silent filter saturation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "expected".
  • Hire: capacity overrun and rebuild.
  • Strong hire: confirm-on-maybe, fill ratio alert, scalable variant.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager asks for "unique visitors per page" on 100,000 pages with 1B pageviews/day. Another stakeholder says the same number will be used to bill advertisers per unique viewer. The data team proposes a SET of user ids per page-day in Redis: estimated 8 GB per day for large pages alone.
questions.promptHtml: What do you build, and what do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use HLL for everything" or "exact sets for everything".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the number used for money or contracts? What error is tolerable? Do we need to list the users? Date ranges (unions)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A, design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: analytics tolerates about 1% error; billing does not.
  4. How I'd verify: compare HLL vs exact on a sampled day.
  5. Root cause of the tension: one metric serving two different accuracy needs.
  6. Fix: dashboards: HLL per page per day (12 KB, standard error about 0.81%): 100k x 12 KB = 1.2 GB, merge days with PFMERGE for weekly. Billing: an exact pipeline (dedupe in the warehouse on (page, user, day)), computed offline and auditable.
  7. Prevention: label metrics "approximate" in the UI; reconcile HLL vs exact monthly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not bill from HLL; do not promise intersections (inaccurate for small overlaps).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Visitors on both page A and B? -> Inclusion-exclusion; poor accuracy for small overlaps.
  • GDPR delete of one user? -> HLL cannot remove; rebuild from source or accept.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard figure became a contractual number and the 1% error turned into a dispute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one approach for both.
  • Hire: HLL for analytics, exact for billing.
  • Strong hire: merge, intersection caveat, labelling and reconciliation.

questions.promptHtml: Compare geohash and quadtree for a nearby-search system, including the edge cases.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Location indexes appear in ride-hailing, delivery and maps; edge cases separate real experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Geohash encodes a lat/lng cell as a string where a shared prefix means nearby, so it's trivial to store in Redis or a DB index and shard by prefix. A quadtree recursively splits space into four, only splitting cells that exceed a point limit, so dense areas (Manhattan) get fine cells and empty areas stay coarse. Geohash is simple and static; a quadtree adapts to density. Both need neighbour-cell queries because of boundary problems.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A 6-character geohash cell is about 1.2 km wide. A 2 km search reads the target cell and its 8 neighbours (up to 9 cells), each holding tens of drivers, instead of scanning 1M.

query(lat,lng,r): c = geohash(lat,lng,6); cells = [c] + neighbours(c)
                  candidates = union(points in cells); filter by true distance <= r

Edge cases: two nearby points can have very different prefixes across a cell boundary (so query neighbours); distortion at the poles; the antimeridian wrap. Sharding by geohash prefix creates hot shards in dense cities; split by load (adaptive quadtree, or S2 cell levels) rather than by area.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Querying only the point's own cell.
  • Sharding by area in a city-dense world.
  • Skipping the final exact distance filter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Update rate? -> 1M drivers every 4 s is 250k writes/s; keep positions in memory or Redis, not a relational table.
  2. Quadtree leaf limit? -> For example 100 points; tune by density.
  3. Why not geohash with variable precision? -> Possible; precision by density needs logic, which is what a quadtree gives.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "prefix match". Senior: neighbours, boundary issues, hot-shard splitting, update throughput.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A ride-hail team had full-city shards at one geohash prefix and rebalanced by load.

questions.contextHtml:
The feed uses pure fan-out on write. A celebrity with 50M followers posts. Fan-out workers process 100k writes/s. Queue metrics:

fanout_queue_depth: 0 -> 38M over 6 min
feed_write_latency p99: 40ms -> 9s
normal users' posts delayed 8-12 min
Redis cluster CPU 91%

Support: "my friends' posts are missing". An engineer proposes doubling workers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add workers and Redis nodes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Follower distribution? How often do celebrities post? Freshness SLA for celebrity posts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop fanning out this account (flag it as celebrity); put its post in a separate store; prioritise normal users' queue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: one 50M fan-out takes 50M / 100k = 500 s (about 8 min) and blocks the shared queue; Redis CPU saturated by those writes.
  4. How I'd verify: queue depth by author, top authors by fan-out size.
  5. Root cause: pure push has write amplification proportional to followers; head-of-line blocking in a shared queue.
  6. Fix: hybrid: push for authors under a threshold (for example 10k followers), pull for celebrities. The celebrity post is stored once; each follower's read merges the feed list with recent posts of the few celebrities they follow (about 2 extra Redis calls). Reads spread over hours. Separate queues by author class.
  7. Prevention: threshold tunable, alert on fan-out size per post.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not just scale: cost grows linearly with followers. Hybrid adds read-path complexity and merge latency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User follows 500 celebrities? -> Cap or sample, cache merged results.
  • Threshold choice? -> From the follower distribution and write capacity; revisit regularly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single post from a large account delayed everyone's feed by 10 minutes before authors were classified.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale workers.
  • Hire: hybrid push/pull with math.
  • Strong hire: head-of-line blocking, separate queues, merge cost, thresholds.

questions.contextHtml: Trending hashtags over 1B events/hour with 100M distinct tags in the window. The exact HashMap approach needs about 5 GB per server (50 B per tag) and several servers each see a subset. Product wants the top 20 per hour per region, near real time, errors on rare tags acceptable. A teammate proposes Count-Min Sketch alone, a second proposes sampling 1%.
questions.promptHtml: Design it and explain the error behaviour.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CMS gives the top-K" with no heap; or ignores overcount.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Accuracy for the top 20? Window type (tumbling vs sliding)? Region cardinality? Latency target?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: CMS for counts plus a min-heap of K candidates; sampling loses small-but-rising tags.
  4. How I'd verify: compare against exact counts offline for one hour.
  5. Root cause of the approach: exact counting costs memory proportional to distinct tags.
  6. Fix: epsilon = 0.0001, delta = 0.01 gives w = e/epsilon = about 27,183 and d = ln(1/delta) = about 5 rows; 5 x 27k x 4 B = about 540 KB per sketch. On each event update the sketch, estimate the tag's count, and maintain a heap of the top candidates. Per server sketches merge by cell-wise addition, so regional aggregation is cheap. Error is one-sided: counts only inflated, by up to about epsilon x N with probability 1 - delta (100k on 1B events for rare tags), small relative to heavy hitters.
  7. Prevention: an offline exact job to measure drift; reset sketches per window.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not use for billing or per-user counts; report that low-frequency counts may be inflated. Sliding windows need rotating sketches.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Heavy hash collisions? -> Larger w or conservative update.
  • A spike from a new tag? -> It enters the heap once its estimate exceeds the heap minimum.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 540 KB sketch replaced a 5 GB map with the same top 20.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sampling only or exact map.
  • Hire: CMS plus heap, with merge.
  • Strong hire: epsilon/delta math, one-sided error, windows.

questions.contextHtml:
Ride-hail location service: 1M drivers, an update each 4 s (250k writes/s), sharded by 4-character geohash prefix across 24 Redis shards. After launching in a big city, one shard shows 100% CPU while others sit at 15%. Complaints: "no drivers nearby" at cell borders even when drivers are 300 m away across the street.

shard-07 (prefix 'ttnf'... dense downtown) ops/s 61k  p99 480ms
shard-12 ops/s 4k
nearby(lat,lng,2km) returns drivers only from the query point's own cell

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add Redis nodes to the same prefix scheme.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Cell precision used? Read vs write split? Query radius? Can positions be coarsened?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Split the hot prefix by a finer geohash precision across more shards; scale reads with replicas.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) area-based sharding gives hot shards in dense cities; (b) queries ignore neighbour cells.
  4. How I'd verify: per-shard ops, per-prefix counts; a test with points across a boundary.
  5. Root cause: sharding by geographic area instead of by load; missing neighbour query (boundary problem).
  6. Fix: query the cell plus 8 neighbours (6-char cell is about 1.2 km, so a 2 km search reads up to 9 cells with tens of drivers each) then filter by exact distance. Shard by load: adaptive quadtree or S2 level choice, splitting a dense cell into children when it exceeds a point or write limit.
  7. Prevention: per-cell load metric and automatic split alerts; tests at cell borders, poles, antimeridian.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not shard strictly by city; do not drop the exact-distance filter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Driver crosses a cell? -> Remove from the old cell, add to the new one atomically or via TTL entries.
  • Stale positions? -> TTL keys of about 10-15 s.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch day downtown shard melted while three suburbs idled; splitting by load fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add nodes.
  • Hire: neighbour cells and finer split.
  • Strong hire: load-based adaptive sharding, TTLs, edge-case tests.

questions.contextHtml: Design "post analytics" for 1M active posts: total views (high rate), unique viewers per day, top referrers, "has this user already seen this post?" for the feed, and "events near me". Budget: a small Redis cluster. Peak 40k views/s across posts, one viral post at 50k views/s alone. The interviewer says "do not say approximate for everything".
questions.promptHtml: Pick structures per metric and give the memory estimate.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One approach (SQL counts) for all metrics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which metrics are billable? Tolerated error? Retention? Do we need to list viewers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: match each metric to the cheapest structure that meets its accuracy.
  4. How I'd verify: compare against exact on a sample.
  5. Root cause of tension: accuracy vs memory per metric.
  6. Fix: views: sharded counters (exact-ish; shard only hot posts, sum on read); uniques: HLL per post per day (12 KB); top referrers: Count-Min Sketch plus heap (about 100 KB); "already seen": Bloom filter per user in Redis; nearby events: geohash. Memory per post-day: counters 1 KB + HLL 12 KB + sketch 100 KB = about 113 KB, so 1M posts is about 113 GB, shardable across a small cluster. Prefer exact structures first for billing-relevant counts.
  7. Prevention: reconciliation jobs, documented error bounds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not apply approximations where the business needs exact (billing); introduce them only where the stated error is acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retention for 90 days? -> Keep daily HLLs, merge for ranges; compact old data in the warehouse.
  • Bloom per user growth? -> Size per user window, rebuild periodically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Memory estimates per post-day made the cost conversation easy and killed a 10x over-engineered plan.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one tool for all.
  • Hire: correct structure per metric.
  • Strong hire: memory math, exact where needed, reconciliation.
